name: Jaw exerciser
lead: A jaw exerciser is a handheld or mouth-worn resistance device, usually made of silicone or plastic and often shaped like a ball, bar or pair of plates, that the user bites or chews against to train the muscles of mastication, chiefly the masseter. Products in this category are sold under names such as Jawzrsize and are promoted on social media for a more defined jawline and reduced double chin. [1][2][3] The same term and similar devices also exist in clinical practice, where jaw exercisers are used in rehabilitation of restricted mouth opening. [4][5][6]

The masseter is a thick muscle that raises the lower jaw and attaches at the angle of the mandible. Wikipedia reports that the muscle can enlarge in people who habitually clench or grind their teeth and in those who constantly chew gum, and that this enlargement is generally soft and painless. [7] The idea behind cosmetic jaw exercisers is that a larger masseter will change the appearance of the lower face. [3][8]

A 2024 case report of two people who used a commercial jaw exerciser for about three months found no noticeable changes in jaw appearance, and its authors reported that a review of the literature found limited evidence that these devices reduce double chins, enhance jawlines or tighten facial skin, noting that the mastication muscles do not directly affect submental fat or skin elasticity. [3] No controlled trial of cosmetic jaw exercisers on jawline definition was found. Studies on masticatory muscle stiffness and oxygen dynamics after chewing exist, but they concern gum chewing, not these devices. [9][10]

paras: Cosmetic jaw exercisers are used by biting, squeezing or chewing against a firm resistance for sets of repetitions. Some are balls placed between the teeth, some are bars or two-plate devices, and others are mouthpieces moulded around the teeth. Patent filings for jaw exercisers describe devices of widely different purposes, including a 1991 jaw exerciser applying controlled force for facial orthopedics, a 1999 custom-fit strengthener moulded over the teeth, and a 2007 device with opposing plates and a handle to alleviate temporomandibular joint pain. [12][13][14]

In oral and maxillofacial surgery, jaw exercisers have been used for decades after procedures for temporomandibular joint ankylosis and similar conditions to maintain mouth opening. A 1975 paper described a new jaw exerciser for postoperative use in ankylosis, case reports from 1985 and 1986 described a jaw exerciser for fibrous ankylosis, and a case report on oral submucous fibrosis described mouth-opening exercises with a jaw exerciser for six months after surgery, with mouth opening maintained at 32 mm at 18 months. [4][5][6][11] These clinical uses are rehabilitative and are not studies of cosmetic effect.

The 2024 case report describes a commercially available exerciser of the inexpensive silicone mouthpiece type, bought online for about $10, that sits in the mouth and is bitten against, and records user complaints about suction, gagging and a rubbery feel. [41] Related products and ideas circulate under other names: Wikipedia's article on mewing describes a separate, tongue-posture technique devised by orthodontist John Mew and son Mike, which spread through looksmaxxing communities after interest rose from January 2019 and which Wikipedia calls unproven. [42]

The masseter has superficial, deep and coronoid heads and inserts into the angle and ramus of the mandible; it is innervated by the trigeminal nerve and is one of the strongest muscles of mastication. [7] Wikipedia notes that masseteric hypertrophy can occur with bruxism or constant gum chewing and may produce a squarer lower face, and sometimes asymmetry when enlargement is unequal. [7]

Proponents argue that resistance training of the masseter increases its size and definition. The authors of the 2024 case report observe that the muscles worked are not those that determine submental fat or skin tension, and conclude that cosmetic claims about double chin or skin tightening are not well supported. [3] Grokipedia's article on the masseter likewise describes its anatomy and the effects of hypertrophy, although it is an AI-generated source. [8]

Wikipedia's bruxism article lists enlargement of the masseter among signs of habitual clenching, and says botulinum toxin temporarily weakens the muscle, with disuse atrophy possibly reducing later need. [43] These observations are the usual reference point for the idea that loading the muscle changes its size; they concern habitual clenching, not purpose-built devices. The same article notes that patients with masseteric enlargement often seek care because of comments about their appearance. [7][43]

Evidence on cosmetic use is limited to a single report. In a 2024 case report in Cureus, two people used a commercially available jaw exerciser for about three months following the product's instructions; neither reported noticeable changes in jaw appearance by subjective measurement, and the authors reviewed the broader literature and found the overall evidence inconclusive. [3][15] The report involved a 27-year-old man (BMI 30) and a 24-year-old man (BMI 24) who each used the device for about 10 minutes per session, 2-3 and 1-2 times a week respectively, and who judged outcomes from before-and-after photographs; neither saw a change in double chin, jawline or face and neck tightness, and satisfaction ratings were mostly neutral or negative. The authors, who were also the participants, acknowledged limitations including no blinding, no objective measurements and a very small sample, and called for larger studies with objective measures. [41]

Related studies concern gum chewing rather than jaw exercisers. A 2021 study used shear wave elastography to monitor changes in masticatory muscle stiffness after gum chewing, and a 2024 study examined the effect of gum chewing training on masseter muscle oxygen dynamics. [9][10] Clinical reports of jaw exercisers in ankylosis and mouth-opening rehabilitation exist but do not address cosmetic outcomes. [4][6][11][16]

In its literature review, the case report cites a controlled study in which facial exercises did not significantly improve facial rejuvenation, reviews finding that jaw exercises for temporomandibular disorders improve mobility and comfort without a meaningful effect on facial contour, and a study of a different facial muscle device (the Pao) that reported rejuvenation benefits through another mechanism. The authors point to fillers, botulinum toxin, high-intensity focused ultrasound and radiofrequency as alternatives with more evidence for submental contouring. [41]

Wikipedia notes that masseter enlargement can be mistaken for conditions such as salivary gland disease or dental infection, and that habitual clenching and grinding are associated with hypertrophy. [7] Wikipedia's bruxism article says large jaw forces can harm the temporomandibular joints, with pain in front of the ear, clicking and, in severe chronic cases, myofascial pain and joint arthritis, although the link between bruxism and temporomandibular disorder is debated. [43]

Some looksmaxxing posters warn that exercisers could cause TMJ problems. No published trial has measured the rate of such effects from cosmetic jaw exercisers; in the 2024 case report the complaints were about comfort and gagging. [41] Wikipedia also notes uneven masseter growth can produce facial asymmetry. [7] Bruxism and temporomandibular disorders are discussed in the related entry on night guards.

Jaw exercisers are discussed in looksmax.org threads asking which device is best and whether buying exercisers on Amazon will produce masseter hypertrophy. [17][18] A T Nation post from 2013 told a poster to look up Jawzrsize, treating it as a joke solution to a different problem, which illustrates the product's name recognition outside looksmaxxing. [2]

The jawline is a central topic in looksmaxxing communities, where lower-third structure is discussed at length and mewing is a closely related practice. [42] Wikipedia states that the American Association of Orthodontists reports no evidence that mewing improves the jaw, while masseter enlargement from habitual gum chewing or clenching is described separately. [42][7]

lore.intro: Jaw exercisers are discussed on looksmax.org as tools for building masseter size, with threads weighing which devices to buy and whether the result is hypertrophy of the muscle. [17][18]

claims.claim: Jaw exercisers build a bigger masseter and a more defined jawline.
claims.believers: Posters ask which devices are best and whether purchased exercisers can cause masseter hypertrophy. [17][18]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports masseter enlargement in people who clench or chew gum habitually, and a 2024 case report found no noticeable change in jaw appearance after about three months of use by two people. [3][7]

claims.claim: Jaw exercisers reduce a double chin or tighten facial skin.
claims.experts: The case report authors say the chewing muscles do not directly affect submental fat or skin elasticity and that evidence is limited. [3]

claims.claim: Overusing a jaw exerciser can give you TMJ problems.
claims.believers: Some looksmaxxing posters caution that biting devices could strain the jaw joint.
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports that large clenching forces can harm the temporomandibular joints, but no published trial has measured joint effects from cosmetic exercisers. [43]

claims.claim: Chewing tough gum or mastic gum builds the jaw more safely than a device.
claims.believers: Chewing hard gum is described in jawline discussions as a way to build masseter size.
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports masseter enlargement in people who constantly chew gum, generally soft and painless, and studies exist on masticatory muscle stiffness and oxygen dynamics after gum chewing; none tests cosmetic jawline change. [7][9][10]

claims.claim: Mewing and jaw exercises work together for a sharper face.
claims.believers: Looksmaxxing communities that popularised mewing also discuss jaw training. [42]
claims.experts: Wikipedia says no credible scientific research has proven the efficacy of orthotropics, and that the AAO reports no evidence mewing improves the jaw. [42]

angle.text: People use jaw exercisers hoping that a stronger, larger masseter will give the lower face a more defined or squarer jawline, and some products are also marketed for a smaller-looking double chin. The proposed link is muscle growth at the jaw angle; the only published appearance study is a small case report.
